The first sound I recorded for the town of Bellwether was my own stomach. I was standing in the empty council chamber, wearing headphones and holding a microphone toward the ceiling, when a large animal appeared to wake up somewhere under the floor. I tore off the headphones. The room was quiet. I put them back on. The animal gave a long, considered reply.

“Have you had lunch?” asked June Vale, the town clerk.

I admitted I had not.

“Well,” she said, “before we preserve anything for posterity, let’s get you a sandwich.”

The town had received a modest arts grant to make a sound map. Visitors would be able to touch a spot on a screen and hear what happened there: water passing beneath the iron bridge, shoes on the wooden stairs of the library, the high school band practicing behind the gym. I was twenty-six, recently graduated, and the owner of a microphone expensive enough to make people assume I knew how to use it. June hired me for six weeks. The sandwich, she made clear, would come out of her own pocket.

I began with the obvious things. I recorded the noon whistle at the paper mill and the courthouse clock striking four. The clock struck five times, which I noted on the file. At the bakery I captured the slap of dough against a floured bench. At the swimming pool I lowered a waterproof microphone into the deep end and discovered a world of distant knocks and enormous, velvety booms. A little girl asked what I was doing. When I told her, she put her face in the water and shouted, “My name is Frances!”

For several days I went around with the proprietary happiness of a person gathering mushrooms. Other people walked past a drainpipe; I could take it home. I acquired the freight elevator at Lutz Furniture, the pedestrian signal on Elm, the squeaking pivot of the playground horse. I had a folder called BELLS and another called BIRDS and a third, increasingly important folder called PROBABLY BIRDS. In the evenings I sat in my rented room above the pharmacy, listening to Bellwether while Bellwether itself went on outside.

June reviewed my progress on Friday afternoons. She listened without closing her eyes, the way some people taste soup. Her office contained thirty years of council minutes, a rubber plant of exceptional width, and one photograph of a young man in swimming trunks standing beside a canoe. I assumed he was somebody she had lost. On our second Friday he came in wearing a parcel company uniform, took eleven dollars from her purse with permission, and called her Mom.

“These are nice,” June said after he left. “But why have you got the lid of the blue mailbox?”

“It makes a good noise.”

“It does. But nobody here would know it from the lid of a mailbox in Ohio.”

This struck me as a provincial objection to an international standard of hinge. I tried to explain that the map was a portrait, that a portrait required ordinary features as well as distinguishing ones. June ate three peanuts and folded the top of the packet down.

“Go see Mr. Saye,” she said. “Ask him about the applause.”

Mr. Saye lived in a narrow house behind the former picture palace, which had been divided into a carpet showroom and a chapel. He was ninety-one. His daughter led me through a kitchen full of cooling pies to the back porch, where he sat shelling peas into a stainless steel bowl. I set the microphone on the table. He looked at it and began dropping the peas one at a time from a greater height.

“I used to run the films,” he said. “Is that what you’re after?”

I asked about the applause.

“Oh, that wasn’t for the films. That was for Leonard.”

Leonard, it turned out, had driven the last bus from the railway station. On Saturday nights the feature ended at ten forty-five and the bus was due to leave at ten fifty. The theater doors opened onto a side street; the stop stood around the corner on Market. If the credits ran long, somebody would telephone the station and ask the dispatcher to tell Leonard to wait. Leonard always waited. When the doors opened, the audience could see the rear of his bus reflected in the dark window of the jeweler’s shop opposite. If they saw it there, they applauded.

“People clapped for a reflection?” I asked.

“They clapped for the bus. The reflection was how they knew they had one.”

“Did Leonard hear them?”

“He said he could. I think he liked to say he could.”

I asked whether any recording existed. Mr. Saye laughed. “Who’d stand in a doorway holding a tape recorder when he had five minutes to catch a bus?”

That night I labeled the file SAYE, ARTHUR—RECOLLECTION OF APPLAUSE. It was twenty-three minutes long. Near the end, his daughter came out and said the pies were ready. He told her I was from the radio. She said in that case I ought to know his name was Albert.

My project changed after that. At the grocery store I put up a card asking, “What did Bellwether used to sound like?” Replies arrived on the answering machine in June’s office. A woman remembered the milkman carrying empty bottles between his fingers, four in each hand. A retired teacher imitated the particular cough that had passed through assembly whenever the headmaster said “character.” Three callers mentioned a dog named Admiral who sang along with the ice cream van. One of them was prepared to sing both parts.

I still made field recordings, but more often I sat at kitchen tables while somebody tried to put a vanished noise into words. A loom had sounded like a drawer of cutlery falling down stairs, except regular. The old dentist’s drill had been green. Yes, green was a color, the man understood that, but the sound had been green as well. A skating pond made a noise on cold nights like a whale calling through a keyhole. I had never heard a whale or listened through a keyhole. Nevertheless I felt I knew exactly what she meant.

There were disputes. The founders’ parade had begun with a cannon, unless it had begun with a bass drum struck behind the war memorial, unless it had begun, as one indignant letter maintained, with a prayer. The bird outside the post office that said “Peter, Peter” had said “Teacher, teacher” and had lived outside the bank. I stopped trying to settle these matters. On the map I placed three small dots at the parade ground. I drew the line at putting a bird in two places, then remembered that birds could fly.

By the fifth week I had gathered so much material that the map took a full minute to load. June found me at midnight in the council chamber, cutting the silences out of a recording of a woman describing her father coming home from work. First there had been his bicycle bell at the corner, she said. Then the gate. Then nothing for a while, because he always stopped to pull a weed or two. Then his key missing the lock.

“Why did he ring the bell at the corner?” I had asked.

“So we’d put the kettle on.”

June sat down beside me. On my screen, the woman’s voice appeared as a blue thicket broken by level stretches of pale gray.

“You took out the weeding,” June said.

“She wasn’t talking.”

“I know. She was waiting for him to get to the door.”

I put it back. We listened to twelve seconds of an old woman’s refrigerator, a truck passing in the street, and a small click that might have been her wedding ring touching the table. Then the key missed the lock.

“Do you have one?” I asked June.

“A refrigerator?”

“A sound you remember.”

She considered. “My sister could whistle with a blade of grass. She held it between her thumbs.”

“What did it sound like?”

“Terrible. That was the attraction.”

“Could we record you talking about it?”

“No need,” she said. “She lives in Dayton. I can ask her to do it.”

The next morning an audio message arrived from an Ohio number. There was some negotiation with a lawn mower, a long inhalation, and a blast so piercing that a dog began barking several yards away. Then two women laughed, one in my headphones and one at the desk across the room. June pressed the heels of her hands against her eyes. “She’s still got it,” she said.

The public unveiling was scheduled for the last Sunday in August. The hardware store lent us a projector. The chapel lent us fifty folding chairs, each bearing on its underside a small paper label that read CHAPEL, as if an unmarked folding chair might be readily mistaken for private property. We hung a sheet on the wall of the council chamber. At three o’clock June opened the doors, and sixty-eight people came in out of the heat.

I had prepared remarks about acoustic ecology. Looking at the audience, which included Frances from the swimming pool wearing a dress patterned with lemons, I abandoned them. I explained how the map worked. I clicked the iron bridge. Water rushed through the chamber, followed by the hollow tire music of a car crossing overhead. People turned toward the windows. Outside there wasn’t a cloud in the sky.

Then I let the audience choose. We heard the paper mill and Admiral and the underwater declaration of Frances, who received the afternoon’s first round of applause. We listened to Mr. Saye shell peas, though he had stayed home because Sundays were for his family. When I played the clock striking four, the audience counted aloud to five. Somebody called for the dentist. Somebody else called, with feeling, for absolutely anything but the dentist.

About forty minutes in, a boy in the front row pointed to a dot at the edge of the screen. It lay well beyond the town boundary, in a pale empty region where the map software had found nothing worth labeling.

“What’s out there?” he asked.

I knew the dot. During my first week I had driven north to record the railway crossing at Harker’s Field. I had waited an hour without a train. The dot was supposed to be hidden; I had put it on the map as a reminder to go back.

“Nothing much,” I said. “I was waiting for a train that didn’t come.”

“Let’s hear it,” said the boy.

People settled back into their chairs. I clicked.

At first the room filled with a soft continuous shushing. Wind moved through the dry grass beside the track. An insect ticked somewhere close to the microphone. From very far off came two notes of machinery reversing. I stood beside the projector, suddenly conscious of charging the public money to listen to a ditch.

Then, behind me, a man said, “Lapwing.”

Another voice said, “No, that’s the gate on the Ullman place.”

“My God,” a woman whispered. “That is the gate.”

The noise came again: a thin rise, a pause, a thin fall. Perhaps it was a bird. Perhaps somebody a quarter mile away had spent that hot afternoon carrying things through a gate. A minute went by. The recording contained my shoe shifting on gravel, my sleeve brushing the microphone stand. Nobody asked me to skip ahead.

I let it play for four minutes. In the fourth, we heard an approaching engine. It grew louder, passed, and faded. A man near the back took off his cap.

“Anthony,” he said.

Several people turned.

“That’s my brother’s truck. Listen when he changes gear. He’s got that loose bit on the exhaust.”

I dragged the cursor back. The engine approached again. As the driver shifted, a brief metallic jangle rose out of the growl.

“Could be any truck,” said a woman beside him.

“Could be,” he agreed, perfectly happy.

Afterward, while we folded chairs, I asked whether his brother had died. He looked startled. “Anthony? He’s at the lake. Why?”

I said I had misunderstood.

“He owes me a ladder,” the man added, as though this might help me get the story straight.

My contract ended on Tuesday. I packed my headphones and microphone, said goodbye to the pharmacist downstairs, and carried my suitcase to the bus stop on Market. Across the road, the jeweler’s window reflected a white delivery van and half a cloud. June came to see me off. She brought two egg sandwiches wrapped in waxed paper, one for the journey and one against the possibility, never yet disproved, that a young person might be hungry again later.

I asked what she would do with the map. She said the schools wanted a copy. The library would keep the original files. There was enough money left to buy a recorder that people could borrow with a library card.

“Are you going to keep adding things?” I asked.

“If people bring them in.”

The bus rounded the corner. Its brakes gave a descending sigh. For six weeks I had been training myself to hear such noises as potential possessions. My hand went to the side pocket of my bag before I remembered I had packed the microphone under my clothes.

June noticed. “You’ll have to remember that one.”

What I remember now, years later, is not the brakes. I remember the waxed paper warming through against my palm. I remember that the driver had a little electric fan clipped to his dashboard and that its blue blades turned so slowly I doubted they could move any air. I remember June stepping back from the curb, already looking toward the council offices, where there was work to do that had nothing to do with me. As the bus pulled away, I looked into the jeweler’s window and saw my own bus traveling there, full of people going in the same direction at precisely the same speed.

There might have been applause. Of course there wasn’t. But I understood, at last, the practical arrangement: how the people coming out of the picture palace could see, without hurrying yet, that they had time. I hoped they had used a little of it. I hoped somebody had stood under the marquee to finish telling a joke, and somebody else had pretended not to hear the end, so that on the ride home there would be a reason to tell it again.
